blocks.text: The widow’s debt threatens more than the loss of property: the creditor is coming to take her two sons as bondmen. Elisha’s instructions turn the only resource remaining in her house—a pot of oil—into something she can sell. The provision therefore answers the crisis in concrete stages: she can pay what she owes and then support herself and her sons with what remains.

sections.title: Prophetic Help in Household and Communal Crises

blocks.text: The rest of the chapter places Elisha’s prophetic work in both a household and a community. The Shunammite woman’s hospitality leads to the promise of a son, and when that child dies, she travels from Shunem to Carmel to seek Elisha; his response unfolds through the staff sent with Gehazi, prayer, bodily action, and a return to the child. The setting then shifts to a prophetic community suffering during famine: dangerous stew is made harmless, and twenty barley loaves and firstfruits feed a hundred people with food left over. Taken together, these scenes connect the prophetic word and action with threats involving childlessness, death, famine, dangerous food, and scarcity.
